nameStory: This tiny aquatic organism doesn't have a common name - it's known only by its scientific name, Staurodesmus bulnheimii. The genus name 'Staurodesmus' comes from Greek words meaning 'cross-shaped chain,' referring to how these microscopic algae often link together in star-like patterns. It was named after the scientist Bulnheim who first described this particular species.
description: Staurodesmus bulnheimii is a microscopic single-celled green alga that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes. Each cell is incredibly tiny - much smaller than the period at the end of this sentence - and can only be seen clearly with a microscope. The cells have a distinctive flattened, somewhat triangular shape with small projections or 'horns' extending from the corners. These algae are part of a group called desmids, which are known for their beautiful geometric shapes and bright green color.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual cells are only visible under magnification - you'll need at least a hand lens to see them as tiny green specks, and a microscope to see their true shape

idTips.label: Triangular cell shape
idTips.description: Under a microscope, cells appear flattened and roughly triangular with a pinched middle section where the cell appears to be divided in half

idTips.label: Small projections
idTips.description: Tiny spine-like extensions or 'horns' stick out from the corners of each cell, giving it a star-like appearance

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Cells have an intense emerald green color due to their chloroplasts - the same structures that make plants green

idTips.label: Clear cell wall
idTips.description: The cell wall appears glass-like and transparent under the microscope, with the green contents clearly visible inside

habitat: This species lives in clean, unpolluted freshwater environments like pristine ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It prefers slightly acidic to neutral water conditions and is often found in areas with good water quality. Look for it in quiet backwaters where sediment can settle and the water remains relatively still.

seasonality.spring: Population begins to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight increases. This is often the best time to find them as they multiply rapidly in fresh spring water.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though they can still be found in suitable habitats.
seasonality.winter: Populations persist at low levels under ice cover, entering a dormant phase until spring conditions return.

funFact: Despite being single-celled organisms smaller than a grain of salt, these algae are master architects - each species in their group has evolved a unique geometric shape so precise that scientists can identify them just by their cellular 'blueprint,' making them the living equivalent of microscopic snowflakes.
confusionNotes: This species can be easily confused with other Staurodesmus species, which all share similar triangular shapes and small projections. The key differences are in the exact arrangement and length of the spines, the degree of the cell's central constriction, and subtle variations in overall proportions - details that require careful microscopic examination to distinguish.
contextualKnowledge: This organism represents one of nature's most overlooked groups - the desmids are among the most geometrically beautiful life forms on Earth, yet most people never see them because of their microscopic size. They're indicators of clean water, so finding diverse desmid communities suggests healthy aquatic ecosystems.
compareHints: Staurodesmus bulnheimii differs from its relatives by having shorter, more blunt projections compared to species like S. longispinus which has notably long spines. Unlike S. triangularis which has a more pronounced triangular outline, S. bulnheimii tends to have a more rounded triangular shape. The central constriction (pinched middle) is also typically less pronounced than in species like S. cuspidatus.
